paragraphs.quote: When one IPv6 node has a large amount of data to send to another node, the data is transmitted in a series of IPv6 packets. These packets can have a size less than or equal to the Path MTU (PMTU). Alternatively, they can be larger packets that are fragmented into a series of fragments each with a size less than or equal to the PMTU.

paragraphs.quote: It is usually preferable that these packets be of the largest size that can successfully traverse the path from the source node to the destination node without the need for IPv6 fragmentation. This packet size is referred to as the Path MTU, and it is equal to the minimum link MTU of all the links in a path. This document defines a standard mechanism for a node to discover the PMTU of an arbitrary path.

paragraphs.quote: IPv6 nodes should implement Path MTU Discovery in order to discover and take advantage of paths with PMTU greater than the IPv6 minimum link MTU [RFC8200]. A minimal IPv6 implementation (e.g., in a boot ROM) may choose to omit implementation of Path MTU Discovery.

A node sending packets much smaller than the Path MTU allows is wasting network resources and probably getting suboptimal throughput.

paragraphs.quote: This memo describes a technique to dynamically discover the PMTU of a path. The basic idea is that a source node initially assumes that the PMTU of a path is the (known) MTU of the first hop in the path. If any of the packets sent on that path are too large to be forwarded by some node along the path, that node will discard them and return ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages. Upon receipt of such a message, the source node reduces its assumed PMTU for the path based on the MTU of the constricting hop as reported in the Packet Too Big message. The decreased PMTU causes the source to send smaller packets or change EMTU_S to cause the upper layer to reduce the size of IP packets it sends.

paragraphs.quote: It is therefore suggested that the IP layer store PMTU information and that the ICMPv6 layer process received Packet Too Big messages. The packetization layers may respond to changes in the PMTU by changing the size of the messages they send. To support this layering, packetization layers require a way to learn of changes in the value of MMS_S, the "maximum send transport-message size" [RFC1122].
paragraphs.reason: PMTU state lives in Connection rather than the suggested IP-layer cache, and there is no generic MMS_S-change interface to other packetization layers. Extension-header parsing is not the reason for this storage/service gap.

paragraphs.quote: MMS_S is a transport message size calculated by subtracting the size of the IPv6 header (including IPv6 extension headers) from the largest IP packet that can be sent, EMTU_S. MMS_S is limited by a combination of factors, including the PMTU, support for packet fragmentation and reassembly, and the packet reassembly limit (see "Fragment Header", Section 4.5 of [RFC8200]). When source fragmentation is available, EMTU_S is set to EMTU_R, as indicated by the receiver using an upper-layer protocol or based on protocol requirements (1500 octets for IPv6). When a message larger than PMTU is to be transmitted, the source creates fragments, each limited by PMTU. When source fragmentation is not desired, EMTU_S is set to PMTU, and the upper-layer protocol is expected to either perform its own fragmentation and reassembly or otherwise limit the size of its messages accordingly.
paragraphs.reason: Supported base IPv6 headers and TCP options are budgeted without source fragmentation, but accounting for IPv6 extension-header lengths is unsupported. Source fragmentation is an explicitly conditional alternative, not itself a required missing capability.

paragraphs.quote: However, packetization layers are encouraged to avoid sending messages that will require source fragmentation (for the case against fragmentation, see [FRAG]).
paragraphs.reason: Enabled TCP limits complete IPv6 packets to the path budget rather than invoking source fragmentation; the family-floor test parses base-header packets and checks resized retry length with timestamp options. Extension headers and shared caches are not prerequisites of this avoidance recommendation.

It is left to the implementation to select the local representation of a path. For nodes with multiple interfaces, Path MTU information should be maintained for each IPv6 link.

paragraphs.quote: If the stale PMTU value is too large, this will be discovered almost immediately once a large enough packet is sent on the path. No such mechanism exists for realizing that a stale PMTU value is too small, so an implementation should "age" cached values. When a PMTU value has not been decreased for a while (on the order of 10 minutes), it should probe to find if a larger PMTU is supported.
paragraphs.reason: Enabled IPv6 core holds PTB for 600 seconds and defaults converged-search aging to 600 seconds, reopens the upper search bound on expiry, and emits an ACK-confirmed larger probe. The dual-family real-probe test exercises periodic retry; configurable periodic aging is separately covered at 8201-069.

paragraphs.quote: Note: an implementation should provide a means for changing the timeout duration, including setting it to "infinity". For example, nodes attached to a link with a large MTU that is then attached to the rest of the Internet via a link with a small MTU are never going to discover a new non-local PMTU, so they should not have to put up with dropped packets every 10 minutes.
paragraphs.reason: Reviewed 0030a96: PmtudPolicy exposes SearchAging::Seconds (validated >=300 with checked caller-timebase conversion) and Infinity through creation and live Endpoint::set_pmtud_policy. Tests exercise finite rearming, disabled periodic aging and both families retaining independent mandatory 600-second PTB hold and failure cooldown. No route/cache or socket-parser integration is claimed.

paragraphs.quote: A packetization layer (e.g., TCP) must use the PMTU for the path(s) in use by a connection; it should not send segments that would result in packets larger than the PMTU, except to probe during PMTU Discovery (this probe packet must not be fragmented to the PMTU). A simple implementation could ask the IP layer for this value each time it created a new segment, but this could be inefficient. An implementation typically caches other values derived from the PMTU. It may be simpler to receive asynchronous notification when the PMTU changes, so that these variables may be also updated.
paragraphs.reason: Connection uses the PMTU-derived budget for ordinary data/retries and a distinct bounded real-data probe size. Dual-family wire tests check the exact larger probe and unchanged effective PMTU before ACK; base-header IPv6 packets are unfragmented. IP-service polling is an optional implementation example.

paragraphs.quote: A TCP implementation must also store the Maximum Segment Size (MSS) value received from its peer, which represents the EMTU_R, the largest packet that can be reassembled by the receiver, and must not send any segment larger than this MSS, regardless of the PMTU.
paragraphs.reason: IPv6 core stores peer MSS separately, defaults1220, caps transmit size independently of local link and retains receive MSS1460.

paragraphs.quote: The value sent in the TCP MSS option is independent of the PMTU; it is determined by the receiver reassembly limit EMTU_R. This MSS option value is used by the other end of the connection, which may be using an unrelated PMTU value. See Section 5, "Packet Size Issues", and Section 8.3, "Maximum Upper-Layer Payload Size", of [RFC8200] for information on selecting a value for the TCP MSS option.
paragraphs.reason: IPv6 core stores peer MSS separately, defaults1220, caps transmit size independently of local link and retains receive MSS1460.

paragraphs.quote: Reception of a Packet Too Big message implies that a packet was dropped by the node that sent the ICMPv6 message. A reliable upper- layer protocol will detect this loss by its own means, and recover it by its normal retransmission methods. The retransmission could result in delay, depending on the loss detection method used by the upper-layer protocol. If the Path MTU Discovery process requires several steps to find the PMTU of the full path, this could finally delay the retransmission by many round-trip times.
paragraphs.reason: Explains ordinary reliable-transport loss recovery and its latency. The selected immediate-on-decrease alternative is separately audited in 8201-074; this is not an unchanged-cwnd requirement.

paragraphs.quote: Alternatively, the retransmission could be done in immediate response to a notification that the Path MTU was decreased, but only for the specific connection specified by the Packet Too Big message. The packet size used in the retransmission should be no larger than the new PMTU.
paragraphs.reason: Validated feedback updates the matched Connection and emits a retry no larger than the new IPv6 PMTU; the dual-family floor test checks sequence, payload and full packet length. Exact dropped-range notification is distinct and remains open in 8201-064/066.

paragraphs.quote: Note: A packetization layer that determines a probe packet is lost needs to adapt the segment size of the retransmission. Using the reported size in the last Packet Too Big message, however, can lead to further losses as there might be smaller PMTU limits at the routers further along the path. This would lead to loss of all retransmitted segments and therefore cause unnecessary congestion as well as additional packets to be sent each time a new router announces a smaller MTU. Any packetization layer that uses retransmission is therefore also responsible for congestion control of its retransmissions [RFC8085].
paragraphs.reason: IPv6 lost_probe_repairs uses real receiver ACKs and ntcp-ip6 parsing to assert repairs split within the original probe gap and conservative packet budget, including two decreasing exact original PTBs down to1280 and wrapping sequences. Normal repair admission remains active; finite full-tail proof suppresses only the logical loss response, preserving MSS scaling and the PTB hold. Other-loss, ECN, repair-copy-loss and timeout matrices retain normal retransmission congestion control. Literal unchanged-cwnd and shared-path fanout obligations remain separate.

paragraphs.quote: A loss caused by a PMTU probe indicated by the reception of a Packet Too Big message must not be considered as a congestion notification, and hence the congestion window may not change.
paragraphs.reason: Matching PTB now preserves finite isolated-probe proof and suppresses a congestion-loss response only after receiver delivery and recovery exit. Accepted lower PMTU still calls refresh_path_mss and Congestion::set_mss, rescaling the byte congestion window when MSS decreases; the dual-family receiver matrix asserts that ratio. Thus the literal unchanged-cwnd obligation remains TODO despite the separate RFC4821 congestion-classification closure; required MSS rescaling is preserved.

paragraphs.quote: Some transport protocols are not allowed to repacketize when doing a retransmission. That is, once an attempt is made to transmit a segment of a certain size, the transport cannot split the contents of the segment into smaller segments for retransmission. In such a case, the original segment can be fragmented by the IP layer during retransmission. Subsequent segments, when transmitted for the first time, should be no larger than allowed by the Path MTU.
paragraphs.reason: Non-repacketizing transport protocol actor; TCP retransmissions can be split and no IP fragmentation service is provided.

paragraphs.quote: Path MTU Discovery for IPv4 [RFC1191] used NFS as an example of a UDP-based application that benefits from PMTU Discovery. Since then, [RFC7530] states that the supported transport layer between NFS and IP must be an IETF standardized transport protocol that is specified to avoid network congestion; such transports include TCP, Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) [RFC4960], and the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP) [RFC4340]. In this case, the transport is responsible for ensuring that transmitted segments (except probes) conform to the Path MTU, including supporting PMTU Discovery probe transmissions as needed.
paragraphs.reason: Original mixed paragraph preserved verbatim; exact operative subspans below distinguish host behavior, other actors and selected-algorithm scope. Unselected or explanatory text is not a missing implementation.

paragraphs.quote: It is suggested that an implementation provides a way for a system utility program to:
paragraphs.reason: Introduces the per-path utility controls in 8201-080/081; there is no system-utility path-control interface.

paragraphs.quote: - Specify that Path MTU Discovery not be done on a given path.
paragraphs.reason: PMTUD is configured per connection at creation; no system-utility per-path discovery-disable control exists.

paragraphs.quote: - Change the PMTU value associated with a given path.
paragraphs.reason: Endpoint::set_destination_route and set_route_mtu configure same-path transport ceilings rather than an arbitrary learned path PMTU estimate. Removing or raising a ceiling does not raise effective PMTU without ACK proof, and no system-utility PMTU-cache setter is exposed; lower_mss is another independent send ceiling.

paragraphs.quote: The former can be accomplished by associating a flag with the path; when a packet is sent on a path with this flag set, the IP layer does not send packets larger than the IPv6 minimum link MTU.
paragraphs.reason: Connections configured with PMTUD disabled enforce the IPv6 minimum-MTU send ceiling, including options and retries. No administrative per-path discovery-disable flag or IP-layer path utility interface exists; the connection creation profile does not provide that missing path control.

paragraphs.quote: This Path MTU Discovery mechanism makes possible two DoS attacks, both based on a malicious party sending false Packet Too Big messages to a node.
paragraphs.reason: Explanatory background, terminology, example, cross-reference or bibliography; operative behavior is inventoried in the selected spans, not inferred from keyword occurrence.

paragraphs.quote: In the first attack, the false message indicates a PMTU much smaller than reality. In response, the victim node should never set its PMTU estimate below the IPv6 minimum link MTU. A sender that falsely reduces to this MTU would observe suboptimal performance.
paragraphs.reason: Same enabled-core floor invariant as 8201-034: sub1280 feedback is discarded and a legal 1280 report is accepted. The dual-family wire test asserts both outcomes; no native IPv6 socket or complete threat-model claim.

paragraphs.quote: In the second attack, the false message indicates a PMTU larger than reality. If believed, this could cause temporary blockage as the victim sends packets that will be dropped by some router. Within one round-trip time, the node would discover its mistake (receiving Packet Too Big messages from that router), but frequent repetition of this attack could cause lots of packets to be dropped. A node, however, must not raise its estimate of the PMTU based on a Packet Too Big message, so it should not be vulnerable to this attack.
paragraphs.reason: The strictly-decreasing feedback guard prevents the described increase attack. IPv6 base-header wire test from 819b8f2 rejects equal/larger MTUs before and after a valid decrease, including wrap. The hypothetical router round-trip is not claimed as a separate implemented behavior; no native IPv6 socket or extension-header claim.
